Reflogs record reference-tip updates in the local repository. The default show action lists them, and the HEAD reflog also records branch switching. Those records are files under logs/ in the repository. The page statement that this history is not pushed is that locality; the catalog has no git-push manual.

ref@{n} selects the n-th prior reflog value, so a larger n is older and the selector requires $GIT_DIR/logs/<ref>. HEAD~n is a different selector: the n-th first-parent ancestor. The page tells the reader to confirm the reflog target before moving a branch.

A commit found through the reflog can be given a new branch without switching to it, the current branch can be reset to it, or its change can be reapplied with cherry-pick. The page presents those three choices.

Reachable reflog entries expire on gc.reflogExpire, default 90 days, and unreachable entries on gc.reflogExpireUnreachable, default 30 days. git gc prunes loose objects older than two weeks by default. The page states only the qualitative difference and the existence of grace periods.

git branch -d or -D deletes that branch and its reflog. git branch <name> <start> creates the branch and does not switch to it. The HEAD reflog records branch switching, so a prior checkout may still identify the deleted tip. The page says may.

git revert records a new commit that reverses the selected change and leaves the original commit in history. The manual points reset --hard at discarding uncommitted work, which is a different operation. Choosing revert for shared history is the page collaboration rule built on that difference.

git revert accepts --continue after a conflict, and the shared sequencer text says --continue resumes a failed revert or cherry-pick after the conflicts are resolved. The page says to stage the resolution and continue rather than switch to reset.

git revert -m <parent> selects the mainline parent, numbered from 1. Later merges bring in only changes from commits that are not ancestors of the reverted merge. The faulty-merge howto shows that merging the updated side branch does not restore the reverted changes and does not un-join the histories. git merge prints Already up to date when every named commit is already an ancestor of HEAD. The page states the ancestry result and does not quote that porcelain string. Its usually for parent one follows the howto -m 1 example and is explicitly hedged.

Without --staged, git restore reads the index into the working tree. With --staged, it reads HEAD into the index only. --source names a different tree for the working tree. The page replicas 1/2/3 contrast is that split.

git checkout <tree> -- <path> replaces the worktree path from that tree and adds it to the index. git checkout -- <path> replaces the path from the index. The -- separates the path. The page no longer calls these the same destination as restore --source.

git restore --staged restores only the index, from HEAD by default, and leaves the working file. Pro Git names the resulting status sections: index versus HEAD is Changes to be committed, and index versus worktree is Changes not staged for commit.

git cherry-pick applies the change from the named existing commit and records a new commit. It does not walk a range unless asked, so it does not merge the source branch. A new commit is a child of the current HEAD, so a different parent generally produces a different hash. The page diagram states that copy, not a moved source branch.

If the patch does not apply, cherry-pick stops, leaves HEAD at the last successful commit, sets CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, and writes conflict markers. --continue resumes after the resolution is staged. The page also says to test the destination integration; that is teaching, not a manual requirement.

Because cherry-pick does not traverse history, dependent commits have to be named in dependency order. A redundant commit stops under the default --empty=stop and is not recorded as an empty commit. An initially empty commit fails unless --allow-empty or --empty=keep is set. Creating a new branch leaves the experimental branch in place.

git log --left-right --cherry-mark A...B uses the three-dot symmetric difference, prefixes the sides with < and >, and marks patch-equivalent commits with =. git-log includes the rev-list options that define those flags.

The decision framework matches the command contracts: restore changes selected paths, reset moves local branch state and then the selected trees, revert adds an inverse commit for shared history, and cherry-pick copies selected changes. The inspect-before-and-after habit is the page procedure around those contracts.

The four hands-on fences, executed unchanged in a disposable repository, create the base plus three feature commits, git reset --hard HEAD~3 leaves only the base commit and removes hpa.yaml, HEAD@{1} is the CPU-threshold commit, git reset --hard HEAD@{1} returns that same tip, and cherry-picking feature-scaling~1 then feature-scaling adds those two changes on main as new commits while deployment.yaml stays the base file and the source tip stays put. This is the lead practice-frozen execution on this page digest with git 2.56.0, not a rerun by this verifier.

The three diagrams illustrate reset movement, revert ancestry, and a cherry-pick copy. The reset diagram says --hard moves HEAD and resets the index and working files, --mixed moves HEAD and resets the index, and --soft moves HEAD only. Conceptual hashes are labeled illustrative. The three-tree nickname and its collection-of-files limit are the Pro Git wording.

Client-strategy kubectl apply prints the object that would be sent and does not send it. In kubectl 0.35 apply.go, info.Get runs before the DryRunClient branch, a non-NotFound Get error is returned as a from-server failure, and both Create and the patch path are skipped for DryRunClient. The command builds its REST mapper and namespace from the kubeconfig loader, whose default flag value is an empty kubeconfig path and whose loader starts from the default loading rules. The page separates this command from the Git fragments and requires a complete manifest. The lead run of these exact command bytes did not persist the complete Deployment.
